items.mnemonic: A crossed stem with a swirl below – hiding in the swirl is a lowercase a: a (father).

exampleWord.target: ありがとうございます

items.mnemonic: Two little strokes standing side by side – like the double i in Hawaii: i (ee, as in see).

exampleWord.english: No, I'm not a student. I'm an office worker.

items.mnemonic: A face in profile, lips pushing out to say oo – u (food).

exampleWord.english: There is bread on the table.

items.mnemonic: A short flick above an energetic figure that twists and kicks out mid-exercise – e (end).

exampleWord.english: No, I'm not a student. I'm an office worker.

items.mnemonic: Like あ (a), but the swirl closes into a round o, with a small splash off the top right – o (go). The splash is the giveaway.
A leg mid-karate-kick, with a flick of motion beside it – ka.
An old key – two crossbars on a stem with a little curl below: ki (key).

exampleWord.english: That over there is the station.

items.mnemonic: An open beak pointing left – a cuckoo mid-call: ku (coo).

exampleWord.english: Tomorrow I'm going to the airport by taxi.

items.mnemonic: A barrel strapped to a post – a keg: ke.
Two short strokes stacked – two coins: ko.

exampleWord.english: Tomorrow I'm going to the airport by taxi.

items.mnemonic: き (ki) with one crossbar missing – count the bars: one for sa, two for ki.
A long lock of hair with a flick at the end – she has long hair: shi. Heads-up: the S row bends here, si becomes shi.
A vertical stem with a curl swirling round it – a straw stirring a drink: su (soo).

exampleWord.english: Please speak a little more slowly.

items.mnemonic: A wide mouth with a fang bending down at the right – it says se (set).

exampleWord.english: My younger brother is a high school student.

items.mnemonic: A single thread zigzagging down – sewing stitches: so (sew).
Squint: a lowercase t on the left, a broken a on the right – it spells ta.
さ (sa)'s mirror image – and the T row bends here: not ti but chi (cheese).

exampleWord.english: My father is an office worker.

items.mnemonic: A low curling wave – tsunami: tsu. Another bend in the row: not tu but tsu (the ts in cats, plus u).
A tabletop with one curving leg – te (table).
A stubbed toe with a splinter sticking in – to (toe).

exampleWord.english: My younger brother is a high school student.

items.mnemonic: A cross above, a kneeling figure below – a nun at prayer: na.

exampleWord.english: What do you eat every morning?

items.mnemonic: A needle standing beside two stitches (こ) – ni (needle).
A tangle of noodles with a loop caught at the end – nu (noodle).

exampleWord.english: I have a dog and a cat.

items.mnemonic: A cat sitting by a post, tail curled into a loop – ne, the first sound of neko (cat).

exampleWord.english: My older sister is a teacher.

items.mnemonic: One smooth loop with a slash through it – a NO sign: no.

exampleWord.english: My friend is a clerk at a cafe.

items.mnemonic: A capital H with a little a curled at its foot – ha. As the topic particle it reads wa (kore wa – as for this).
A single stroke swinging down and back up like a wide grin – hee!: hi.
Loose strokes drifting like puffs of air – the H row softens here: fu, a soft f blown between the lips, halfway to hu.
A low hill – you head up and over it: he (hen). As the direction particle it reads e.
は (ha) wearing an extra bar on top – ho.

exampleWord.english: I am a student of Japanese.

items.mnemonic: Two bars crossing a stem that ties off in a loop – ma (mama). It's は (ha)'s right half with an extra bar.

exampleWord.english: My wife is a bank employee.

items.mnemonic: A curling music note – a loop for the note head, a tail for the stem. Sing it: mi, as in do-re-mi.
A stem with a curled loop like a cow's nose ring – moo: mu.
Two curves crossing to make an almond shape – an eye: me (handily, me is Japanese for eye).
A hook with two crossbars – catch more with two barbs: mo (more).

exampleWord.english: My mother is an office worker too.

items.mnemonic: A yacht heeling in the wind – a slanted sail with a pennant flying: ya (yacht).
A loop swinging right around a stem – a U-turn: yu (you).
A string with a yo-yo spinning at the end – yo.

exampleWord.english: I look forward to working with you.

items.mnemonic: A signal dash above a curled radio dish – ra (radio). The Japanese r is a light tongue-tap, halfway to l (like the quick d in buddy).
Two strokes side by side, the right one trailing long – a river between its banks: ri (river).
A zigzag road ending in a tight loop – a roundabout: ru (route).
ね (ne)'s twin without the loop – the tail just kicks up at the end: re (red).
る (ru) minus its end loop – ro. Loop = ru, no loop = ro.

exampleWord.english: I look forward to working with you.

items.mnemonic: Same post as ね (ne) and れ (re), but the tail rounds into one wide open curve – wa (wide).
A twisting figure mid-cartwheel – を. Said as plain o, and used only as the object particle (hon o yomu – read a book).

exampleWord.english: I eat bread in the morning.

items.mnemonic: One swooping stroke like a cursive n – n. The only kana with no vowel; before b, m or p it drifts toward m (senpai sounds like sempai).
Two small ticks at a kana's shoulder – switch your voice on: k to g, s to z, t to d, h to b. Two ticks = vocal cords buzzing.
A small circle at the shoulder – only the H row takes it, popping h into p. Think of the circle as a little bubble popping: p.
A shrunken や (ya) tucked at another kana's foot – the i drops and ya glues on: き + ゃ melts ki-ya into kya, one beat.
A small ゆ (yu) hanging low – same glue: the i drops and yu slides in, so し + ゅ is shu, one syllable.
A small よ (yo) at the foot – the i drops and yo takes over in a single beat: cho, kyo, sho.
A half-size つ (tsu) with no sound of its own – a tiny catch that doubles the NEXT consonant: き っ て = kitte, with a held beat before the t.
An axe – the top bar is the blade, the long stroke sweeps down as the handle: a for axe.
An easel standing on one straight leg – ee: i. Just two strokes.
A roof with a chimney tick on top – u. It's hiragana う squared off, same sound.
An elevator between two floors – top bar, bottom bar, and the shaft between: e.
A pole with a crossbar and one kicked-out leg – it's hiragana お stripped to straight lines: same o.
A karate kick frozen mid-air, the knee bent sharp at the hook – ka. (It's hiragana か minus the small tick.)

exampleWord.english: My friend is a clerk at a cafe.

items.mnemonic: A key's shaft with two teeth cut across it – ki: key.
A cuckoo poking out of its clock, beak open – ku.

exampleWord.english: Tomorrow I'm going to the airport by taxi.

items.mnemonic: A slanted capital K missing its lower leg – ke. The long flat bar keeps it from collapsing into ク (ku).
A box missing its left wall – sharp corners: ko.
Two saplings sprouting up through the soil line – sa.
Two flat drops and a long stroke drawn UP from the bottom – the upswing of a smile: she, shi. Its lookalike ツ (tsu, next level) is drawn top-down instead.

exampleWord.english: Tomorrow I'm going to the airport by taxi.

items.mnemonic: A slide seen from the side, with a kickstand leg – swoosh down it: su.
A tab pulled sideways through a slot – se. It's hiragana せ minus one stroke, gone angular.
One drop, then the long stroke falls from the top – sewing a stitch downward: so. Its twin ン (n, later) rises instead; stroke direction tells them apart.

exampleWord.english: I want to buy a new computer.

items.mnemonic: ク (ku) with a tongue tucked inside the beak – ta.

exampleWord.english: Tomorrow I'm going to the airport by taxi.

items.mnemonic: A lowercase t with a slanted cap – but Japanese has no ti, so it reads chi. Same chi as hiragana ち.
Two drops falling and the long stroke crashing DOWN from the top – a tsunami: tsu. シ (shi) smiles upward; ツ crashes down.
A telephone pole with two crossbars – te.

exampleWord.english: Won't you play tennis on Sunday?

items.mnemonic: A post with one wedge jutting out – a totem pole: to.
A plus sign with its leg swept out to the left – na. It's literally the first two strokes of hiragana な.
Two flat strokes – and ni is Japanese for two (二). The kana IS the kanji.

exampleWord.english: Won't you play tennis on Sunday?

items.mnemonic: ス (su) with its leg lashed through the body – noodles caught crosswise on a chopstick: nu.
A signpost with a little nest tucked against its trunk – ne: nest.
One single slash – no more, no less: no.
Two strokes parting like wings – ha. It doubles as the kanji for eight (八, hachi).

exampleWord.english: Are you going to the station by bus?

items.mnemonic: A hockey stick mid-hit, the blade kicking up at the bottom – hi. Same hi as hiragana ひ.
A flag rippling with no pole – fu. Blow the f softly between your lips, like hiragana ふ.

exampleWord.english: My friend is a clerk at a cafe.

items.mnemonic: A low hill – hiragana and katakana share this one glyph: he. Nothing new to learn.

exampleWord.english: I write my name with a pen.

items.mnemonic: A pole propped up on both sides – it holds: ho.
A map pin dropped at a slant, with one tick of a shadow – ma.
Three quick strokes – three is mittsu in Japanese: mi. (It comes from the kanji 三.)
A cow's face in three lines – two cheeks and a chin tick: moo, mu.
Two lashes crossing over a winked-shut eye – me. (Me also means eye in Japanese.)
A hook catching two rungs – it's hiragana も with the curls ironed flat: same mo.
A slingshot tilted sideways – ya. (It's hiragana や minus the small tick.)
A capital U drawn with a ruler, standing on its own baseline – yu.
A capital E looking the wrong way – you shout yo! to turn it around: yo.
フ (fu) wearing a flat lid – ra, the lid on a ramen bowl.

exampleWord.english: Let's go to a restaurant on Saturday.

items.mnemonic: Two reeds side by side, the right one longer – ri. Hiragana り minus the curve.
Two strokes, and the right one curls up at the end – a root turning at a river bend: ru.

exampleWord.english: There is bread on the table.

items.mnemonic: A single stroke that drops, then kicks up onto a ledge – re.

exampleWord.english: There is a TV in my room.

items.mnemonic: A square box – a robot's mouth: ro.
フ (fu) grown a wall on its left side – wider now: wa.
フ with a bar through its middle – wo, read as plain o. Rare: it only turns up when the particle o is written in katakana.
One flat drop and the long stroke swept UP from the bottom – ン rises: n. ソ (so) falls from the top; that stroke direction is the whole difference.

exampleWord.english: There is bread on the table.

items.mnemonic: A dash that stretches the vowel before it to double length – コ ko + ー = koo. Katakana's long-vowel mark, everywhere in loanwords: コーヒー (koohii, coffee).

exampleWord.english: I look forward to working with you.
There is a TV in my room.
There is bread on the table.
There is bread on the table.
Let's go to a restaurant on Saturday.
